debacle

dih-BAH-kul -- from a French word for the sudden breaking up of ice on a river. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Debacle is a sudden, complete failure.

The product launch turned into a complete debacle once the app crashed in front of every reporter in the room.

Example

A wedding turns into a debacle within a single afternoon: the outdoor ceremony is rained out, the caterer's van breaks down on the highway, and the sound system shorts out mid-vow.

That sudden pileup of failures ruining an important event is what makes the day a debacle. Unlike 'setback,' which can be a single small problem, debacle describes a total collapse.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fiasco: A fiasco is a complete failure with an extra layer of embarrassment, often a faintly comic one -- the kind of flop people retell at parties. A debacle can be just as total without being funny at all: a sudden, serious collapse of a plan or event.

disaster: A disaster is a sudden event causing great damage or loss -- a flood, a fire, a crash -- and the harm is real no matter whose plan failed. A debacle is specifically a plan or performance failing completely, often suddenly and in public.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

triumph: a great success or victory

achievement: something accomplished successfully

Where it sits · how large and damaging the failure is — setback → debacle → catastrophe

setback vs. debacle: A setback is far milder than a debacle -- one problem that slows a plan down for a while, while a debacle is the sudden, complete collapse of the whole thing.

catastrophe vs. debacle: Catastrophe can feel even larger than debacle: debacle often describes an embarrassing collapse of a plan or event, while catastrophe can describe devastating harm on a much bigger scale, including real danger to people.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — de-

prefix — de-: apart, un- (French)

root — -bacle

root — -bacle: a bar, stick (from French bacler, 'to bar', from Latin baculum, 'a stick or bar')

Put it together

Put it together: French debacler meant 'to unbar, to break up,' originally describing the sudden breaking apart of ice jammed on a river once spring arrived, from de- ('apart') and bacler ('to bar', spelled -bacle here), ultimately from Latin baculum, 'a stick or bar.' A debacle, at its root, is a sudden, forceful breaking-apart -- the same root that gives us bacillus, a rod-shaped microorganism named for its shape.

Use the root in a new word: bacillus

Use the root in a new word: bacillus: Under the microscope, the rod-shaped bacillus was easy to tell apart from its round neighbors.
